title: Differential equations, from cooling to resonance
hook: The current in a coil and resistor switched onto DC settles smoothly, but add a series capacitor and the capacitor's voltage can overshoot the supply and ring. What decides whether it settles or rings?
oneBreath: A differential equation is a rule that ties how fast something changes to the thing itself, and sometimes to time, so its answer is a whole curve, not a number. One store of energy, such as a capacitor discharging or a coil switched onto a supply, settles smoothly at a pace set by one time constant, and a rule with no formula can be stepped along a little at a time. Two stores, such as a spring with a mass or a coil with a capacitor, share one equation whose roots decide whether it creeps back, returns quickest or rings, and pushing it in time with its ringing gives resonance.

ideas.title: A rule for change
ideas.oneLine: A differential equation gives a rate from the quantity itself, as cooling does, so its answer is a curve that follows the rule's slope everywhere.

ideas.title: Decay: separate and integrate
ideas.oneLine: A rate in proportion to what is left, as in a discharging capacitor, separates and integrates to y = Ae^(−t/τ), with time constant τ.

ideas.title: Steady state plus a dying transient
ideas.oneLine: Switch a coil onto a supply and its current is the steady value E ÷ R plus a gap that dies away as decay does.

ideas.title: One small step at a time: Euler's method
ideas.oneLine: Euler's method walks short straight steps along the rule's slope, solving equations that have no formula, and smaller steps drift less from the true curve.

ideas.title: The spring and the circuit: one equation
ideas.oneLine: A damped spring and series RLC circuit obey the same second-order equation, term for term: mass as inductance, damping as resistance, stiffness as 1 ÷ C.

ideas.title: Overdamped, critical and ringing
ideas.oneLine: The roots of mr² + cr + k = 0 decide whether it creeps back, returns quickest without ringing, or rings inside a dying envelope.

ideas.title: Pushing it: resonance, and reading a model
ideas.oneLine: Pushed back and forth, a lightly damped spring or circuit settles to a steady swing, largest when the push nears the frequency it rings at.

calibration.q: A hot part, cooling faster the hotter it is above the room, is losing 3 °C a minute right now. How much will it cool over the next minute?
options: Exactly 3 °C, since that is its rate
More than 3 °C, as cooling gathers pace
A little under 3 °C, as the rate eases
calibration.why: 3 °C a minute is its rate at this instant, not the amount it will lose. As it cools, its gap to the room shrinks, so the rate falls below 3 °C a minute and it cools a little less. Cooling eases off; it never gathers pace.

calibration.q: A coil's current, just switched on, has closed 63% of the gap to its final value after 50 ms. How far along is it after 100 ms?
options: All the way: twice the time does the rest
calibration.why: Each 50 ms closes 63% of whatever gap is left. After the first, 37% remains, and closing 63% of that leaves about 14%, so it is about 86% along. Twice the time does not double the rise, and 95% takes about three such steps.
